heading: Find the base behind the destination name
intro: Start by asking where you would actually sleep. A proposal described as Tena or Misahuallí may use the destination as a regional reference rather than identify a room in the centre. Request the precise property location, the meeting point and the places where activities begin. Then look at the journey between them. The photograph of the Misahuallí riverbank helps introduce the setting, but it does not show every possible accommodation or describe the program you are booking. Compare the two proposals on the same map, marking the base and activity locations separately. This makes the choice tangible before you compare prices or settle on a destination label.
points: Mark meeting and activity points separately.
Compare the base with the advertised destination.

heading: Choose activities through the actual program
intro: Give each proposal the same test: what would you do, where would you do it and who would accompany you? A general mention of river travel or forest exploration can cover different experiences. Ask for named outings, the proposed settings and the role of the guide, along with what is included and what is optional. If a community activity appears in the description, ask who hosts it and how participation works. Keep the comparison centred on the activities you want rather than the longer list. A short, clear program can be easier to assess than a brochure that names many possibilities without explaining which belong to your booking.
points: Compare the named outings and their settings.
Ask who hosts any community experience.

heading: Compare the comfort of specific rooms
intro: Choose the room as carefully as the destination. A town-based stay and a property outside the centre may differ, but their names alone do not explain the bathroom, beds, meal arrangements or services available to your group. Compare the actual categories you are being offered. State the requirements that would affect your decision and ask the provider to confirm them in writing. If photographs show several buildings or room types, identify which belongs to your proposal. Keep agreed requirements with the reservation so they are easy to discuss on arrival. This gives the group a shared expectation without assuming that every Tena or Misahuallí property has the same routine.
points: Identify the room category in each offer.
Confirm essential services and meal arrangements.
Keep agreed requirements with the reservation.

heading: Distinguish town observation from a forest outing
intro: The monkey photograph introduces a scene in Misahuallí with people, a wall and a railing. It is useful because it makes the setting visible: this is not a photograph of a remote forest trail. When wildlife is part of your decision, ask which habitats the actual program visits and how observation is organised. Do not count a photograph or an animal mentioned in a destination description as an included encounter. Tell the provider whether you want interpretation, photography or general exploration, and ask how those interests fit the proposed outings. That conversation is more informative than choosing between destinations on the strength of one appealing wildlife image.
points: Identify the setting of each wildlife activity.
Compare guiding rather than promised sightings.

heading: Count the time you will enjoy at the base
intro: Read the days from arrival through departure. Transfers and meeting arrangements may occupy part of a period that looks like a full day in the package title. Ask how the schedule connects meals, activities, preparation and rest. Compare the usable time in the two proposals rather than assuming that an equal number of nights produces equal opportunities to explore. If you prefer a slower pace, say so before choosing the program. Consider how early starts or a final transfer fit the rest of your journey. The aim is an itinerary your group can comfortably follow, with clear expectations about the time spent travelling and the time spent enjoying the stay.
points: Separate transfers from full activity periods.
Fit the program to the group’s preferred pace.

heading: Choose through a complete written proposal
intro: Bring the comparison together in one place: dates, property, room category, named activities, guiding, meals and the start and end of included transport. Ask each provider to clarify anything that remains unclear. Check how changes are communicated and keep the latest version of the itinerary accessible to everyone travelling. If your onward plans are arranged separately, confirm them with the appropriate operator rather than treating them as part of the lodge package. Once those details are visible, decide which proposal best supports your priorities. You may favour Tena, Misahuallí or a combination, but the reason should come from the actual stay and complete journey you have compared.
points: Compare the same inclusions in both offers.
Choose the proposal that answers your priorities.
